 She’s 72, Widowed, With $1.2 Million in the IRA She Took Over From Her Husband. At 73 the IRS Requires $45,283, and She Reports It on a Single Return
 Jake FitzGerald Sat, November 21, 2026 at 1:07 AM PST 5 min read Quick Read 
 Filing single after her husband's death squeezes her $45,283 RMD into tighter brackets, pushing it into the 12% bracket instead of the 10% a joint return would hit. 
 Without a dependent child at home, she can't use qualifying surviving spouse status, so the joint rates end with the year her husband died. 
 Medicare surcharges kick in above $112,000 of single income, and the RMD counts toward that income, raising her monthly premium.

 A 72-year-old widow who moved her inherited IRA into her own name is a year away from her first required withdrawal. The account held $1.2 million at the end of the year before her first RMD year. When she turns 73 in 2027, the IRS requires her to take $45,283. She reports it as a single filer, and the 2027 single brackets run much tighter than the joint brackets she and her husband used. 
 New Africa / Shutterstock.com How the $45,283 Is Figured 
 Spouses who inherit a traditional IRA can treat it as her own IRA by naming herself the owner or by rolling it into her own IRA. Once the money is in her name, the owner's lifetime RMD rules apply. An owner whose spouse is not the only beneficiary uses the IRS Uniform Lifetime Table, Table III. Owners born from 1951 through 1959 start RMDs at age 73. 
 The math uses one division. The prior year-end balance of $1.2 million is divided by the age-73 distribution period of 26.5, which gives $45,283. 
 She must take her first RMD by April 1 of the year after she reaches 73. Every later RMD is due by December 31. If she waits until April 2028 for the first one, she takes two RMDs in 2028, and both count as income that year.

 Why She Files as Single 
 The year a spouse dies is the last year for which you can file jointly with that spouse. Qualifying surviving spouse status keeps the joint rates for 2 years after the year of death, but only for a taxpayer with a dependent child or stepchild living in her home. A 72-year-old with grown children generally doesn't meet that test, so she files single. 
 Story Continues Where the Withdrawal Lands in 2027 
 The 2027 single standard deduction is $16,600. Subtract that from the RMD and $28,683 is taxable, which hits the 12% bracket that starts above $12,800. The 22% rate applies above $52,025 of taxable income. After the RMD, only $23,342 of other taxable income goes below that line. 
 Pension income, interest and the taxable share of Social Security all count against it. The 24% rate starts above $109,125. These figures leave out the extra deductions for taxpayer 65 and older, which reduce taxable income further. 
 This jump from joint to single brackets is the quiet part of the first-year RMD squeeze, and it lands hardest on surviving spouses with seven-figure pre-tax balances. We walked through how to shrink that bill in the years before the first required withdrawal: The First-Year Tax Bomb .

 Medicare Uses Single Thresholds Too 
 The 2027 Part B premium runs $209.40 a month. The income-related surcharge starts for single taxpayer once income is over $112,000, which raises the monthly premium to $293.10. Higher levels go up to $711.80. The RMD counts toward that income along with everything else she reports. 
 Ways to Lower the Tax on the Withdrawal 
 A qualified charitable distribution sent directly from the IRA to a charity is left out of gross income. The 2027 cap is $114,000, and the amount can count toward her RMD. If she has more than one traditional IRA, she figures the RMD for each account separately but can withdraw the total amount from one or more of the IRAs. 
 Missing the deadline triggers an excise tax of 25% of the shortfall. The rate drops to 10% if she fixes the shortfall within the IRS correction window. 
 Her Required Share Rises Every Year 
 At 74 the Uniform Lifetime divisor falls to 25.5. That raises the required share of her prior year-end balance from about 3.77% at age 73 to about 3.92% at age 74. The divisor shrinks again each year after that. If the account grows, her required withdrawals grow faster than the balance, and so does the income she reports against single brackets and single Medicare thresholds. Before each year begins, check the December 31 balance, the new divisor, and how much room is left below $52,025 and $112,000.
